passage: Omkar came home to the smell of dal and the sound of his father Tushar counting coins at the doorway. "I sold the second bullock so that you could stay at the school in town," Tushar said, not looking up. "Remember that when you feel lazy." Omkar's throat closed. He knew. He saw his father's cracked hands every day. But the words weighed on him like a yoke. It felt as though his whole life had been bought and he was not allowed to want anything else. He ate silently, then sat beside his father on the string cot. "Papa, I'll work hard, I promise, and I'll always show you my marks. But I can't promise what I'll become. I'll decide that when I'm ready." Tushar grunted, but he put his hand on Omkar's shoulder.

qa.q: What did Tushar sell to pay for Omkar's school in town?
How did Omkar feel when his father reminded him of the sacrifice?
qa.a: Indebted and trapped. His throat closed and he felt as though his whole life had been bought and he was not allowed to want anything else.

qa.q: What did Omkar promise, and what did he refuse to promise?
qa.a: He promised to work hard and show his father his marks, but not what he will become. That honours the sacrifice without giving up his whole life plan.

qa.q: How might Tushar feel about what he said and Omkar's answer?
qa.a: Proud and worried about his son, and perhaps relieved to hear honest effort promised. He grunted, but he still put his hand on Omkar's shoulder.

grounding: A parent's sacrifice weighs on the protagonist, who honours it with effort and honesty without promising his whole life plan.

passage:
Thursday night

Abbu came home at eleven again, smelling of the bakery ovens, and fell asleep in his chair with his shoes on. He took the second shift so I could stay at this school. Everyone knows. He tells me whenever I skip revision: "I stand at that oven for you, Harish beta."

I know. I feel it every day. I feel like I owe him my whole life, and some days I feel trapped, like my future is already his.

I told Asif at lunch that I want to study design, not medicine, and Asif said, "Then tell your Abbu, idiot. He's working for you to have choices, na?"

Maybe. Tonight I made a plan. I'll keep my marks up, properly, no shortcuts. And on Sunday, when he's not tired, I'll show him the design course list and tell him the truth. I want to honour what he's doing. I just don't think that means living a life I didn't choose.

qa.q: Where does Abbu work the second shift?
qa.a: Abbu works the second shift at the bakery.

qa.q: What does Harish feel when Abbu reminds him of the oven?
qa.a: Harish feels deeply indebted and grateful, but also trapped, as if his future already belongs to his father.

qa.q: What would you advise Harish before the Sunday talk?
qa.a: Harish could keep his marks up as planned and bring the design course list, so his father sees both effort and a serious alternative.

qa.q: How might Asif see Harish's situation?
qa.a: Asif seems to think Harish's father is sacrificing to give him choices, not to control him, so being honest would respect that sacrifice.

grounding: It shows a teen who feels indebted and trapped by a parent's sacrifice, and decides to honour it with effort and honesty rather than handing over his whole life plan.
